name: lzsa
desc: Lossless packer that is optimized for fast decompression on 8-bit micros
why: A packer built for 8-bit machines, a fun window into retro compression tradeoffs and decompression constraints.

brief.what_it_is: LZSA is a set of byte-aligned lossless compression formats, with a packer that encodes files into them, aimed at very fast decompression on 8-bit CPUs. It takes a file of any size, splits it into blocks of up to 64 KB, and emits a packed file that decompresses back to the original. Matches can reach back up to 64 KB. The README points to decompressors for Z80, 6502, 6809, 8088, i8080, PDP-11, MC68000 and Game Boy, written by various contributors. The packer's executable is named lzsa.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a compression format for retro machines where decompression speed and decompressor size matter most, offering alternatives to LZ4 and ZX7 in 8-bit scenarios. LZSA1 is meant to replace LZ4 and LZSA2 to replace ZX7.
brief.how_it_works: The optimizer searches for the sequence of commands that gives the smallest output while keeping decompression as fast as possible, and the match-finder and optimizer cooperate to prefer 8-bit match offsets. LZSA2 uses 5-, 9-, 13- and 16-bit offsets encoded with nibbles, plus rep-matches, and avoids slow bit-packing in favour of byte alignment and nibbles. The encoding avoids 16-bit arithmetic on the decoder side.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no build, install or usage steps and shows no command lines. The brew formula supplies the lzsa executable. Packing needs nothing special; the decompressors are assembly routines meant for the target 8-bit machines.
brief.standout: The packer's optimizer deliberately spends effort to keep decompression fast on 8-bit CPUs, not just to shrink output, and the authors cite a 67-byte size-optimized Z80 decompressor for LZSA1. Many retro projects have adopted it, including demos, a game port and an assembler.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README shows no release dates, last commit, or maintenance notice, so I could not judge whether the project is active. I did not fetch the repository's commit or release pages.
brief.caveats: The README gives no usage instructions, so the command syntax is unknown from these notes. Benchmark tables are the authors' own and compare against LZ4_HC, ZX7, LZ5, Lizard and MegaLZ. The compressor is about 2X slower than LZ4_HC. Licensing is split: the LZSA code is zlib, and matchfinder.c is CC0 because it reuses parts of Wimlib. Several decompressors are third-party ports with their own origins.
quotes: LZSA is a collection of byte-aligned compression formats that are specifically engineered for very fast decompression on 8-bit systems.
LZSA1 is designed to replace LZ4 and LZSA2 to replace ZX7, in 8-bit scenarios.
The compressor is approximately 2X slower than LZ4_HC but compresses better while maintaining similar decompression speeds and decompressor simplicity.
